citation.title: Can you count on a calculator? The role of agency and affect in judgments of robots as moral agents

reading.source_scope_note: Human observer experiment with fictional robot descriptions and images. Hypothetical delegation preference, explicit trust, competence and responsibility ratings do not measure actual robot moral performance, feelings, legal eligibility or implemented consequential delegation.
access_limits: All19supplied pages and all four meaningful figures read/inspected. The two covers are included in the page count; article locators differ by two pages. Current final-issue PDF was not independently compared.

Publisher full HTML returned403 and its supplement landing was inaccessible through the search tool. A public Figshare resource-doi query identified exact matching article20060115, DOI10.6084/m9.figshare.20060115.v1; canonical metadatahttps://api.figshare.com/v2/articles/20060115.

study.sample: 184Netherlands undergraduate students, mean age20.26SD3.96,34men; no exclusions reported. Course credit plus one randomly drawn€50voucher. Power analysis minimum179rounded180, achieved184. Do not infer that every student or demographic group shares the reported attitudes.
study.design: 2agency(high/low)×2affect(high/low)between-subjects, crossed with2appearance(humanoid/mechanical)within-subjects. Four pictured robots of each type; eight priming-story/dilemma blocks. Assignments based on randomly generated participant number; counterbalanced robot/story/dilemma pairing and pseudo-random appearance order(no more than two identical types in sequence).
study.priming: Agency descriptions emphasize autonomy, thought and self-control; affect descriptions emphasize felt conscious experience. Two comprehension questions focus on mental states/perspective taking in all but the low-low condition, where they target neutral facts. Thus attributed capacities, mental-state elaboration and potential demand cues can vary together.
study.outcomes: After each fictional life-tradeoff dilemma, binary prefer-robot-versus-self decision choice labeled implicit trust, open rationale, and0–100capability/explicit trust/responsibility sliders. The robot is not shown making an actual decision. Responsibility item separately asks to imagine sacrifice of the individual. No actual harm or live authority transfer.
study.post_ratings: Eight capacity-attribution items plus liking, willingness to interact, feeling safe and deserved punishment. Priming text/picture repeated as memory cues. The eight attribution items form one reported exploratory factor, eigenvalue6.01,75.08%variance,alpha.95; this does not independently establish clean two-dimensional agency/affect manipulation checks.
study.models: Binary choices modeled with binomial mixed effects, participant and item random intercepts, and reported convergence-driven random-slope simplification; predictors sum-coded. Explicit trust/capability/responsibility and post ratings analyzed as participant-by-appearance averages via stated doubly multivariate repeated measures approach after correlations. Valid repeated-data methods are not blanket independent-row pseudoreplication.
study.implicit_results: Agency beta.36,Z3.78,p<.001;affect beta.28,Z2.98,p=.003;three-way beta−.16,Z−2.63,p=.008. Supplement appearance beta.15,Z1.46,p=.143. Mechanical subset agency/affect p=.002;humanoid affect p=.058. Actual three-way interaction retained; significance/non-significance alone is not the between-type comparison.
study.explicit_results: Mechanical mean36.10 versus humanoid33.81;appearance F5.67,p=.018. Agency and affect main effects significant;three-wayF4.44,p=.036. For humanoids, either attribute raises ratings relative to low-low while adding the second produces no detected further increase. Means around26–40do not demonstrate a literal scale ceiling.
study.capability_responsibility: Capability agency/affect effects and three-wayF9.10,p=.003;appearance p=.631. Responsibility affectF6.33,p=.013;agency p=.309,appearance p=.904,all interactions nonsignificant. A null agency effect is not universal agency irrelevance or equal responsibility across conditions.
study.safety_punishment: Supplement Table2 reports appearance/agency/affect effects on felt safety; humanoid/affect effects on punishment. These are subjective judgments, not objectively safer robots, warranted sanctions or legal/clinical standards.
study.reporting_limits: Main text repeatedly prints denominator df183 despite184people and a stated full2×2between-subject design, for which conventional complete factorial error df would180. Supplement omits dfs, so exact model/output cannot be reconstructed. Do not fabricate corrected p values or discard robustly reported effects wholesale.
study.source_concessions: Authors acknowledge hypothetical online context, possible moral-choice/blame offloading, and possible demand effects. Similar explicit/implicit patterns do not rule out competing motives; a between-subjects design alone does not eliminate demand effects.
study.not_established: No causal mediation model, independent actual agency/experience verification, consciousness, moral legitimacy, uncanny-valley curve, identity-threat mediator, actual care/punishment learning, psychiatric diagnosis or jurisdiction-specific insanity rule.

summary: No new behavior rows. Clarify Moral trust as an explicit umbrella for distinct source-defined moral reliance and value endorsement; enrich existing capacity/delegation/anthropomorphism records. Preserve formal interactions and actual nulls, correct swapped figure meanings and wrong bibliographic pointers, and exclude unsupported clinical/legal/punishment extrapolation.

findings.definition: Willingness to rely on an agent’s moral judgment or endorse its ethical commitments.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The source operationalizes moral trust through a binary hypothetical decision/delegation preference and a 0–100 explicit right-decision trust rating. Both respond to attributed agency/affect, with actual three-way interactions. Appearance favors mechanical robots for explicit trust, while the implicit appearance main effect is nonsignificant (supplement p=.143). These measures differ from the value-endorsement usage in review 121.
findings.boundary: This catalogue uses an umbrella for source-specific moral-decision reliance and endorsement of an advisor’s values. These are not interchangeable measures or proven identical mechanisms. The present study’s so-called implicit trust is an explicit hypothetical delegation choice, not an unconscious test. Neither a rating nor endorsement establishes genuine ethical commitments, actual capability, consent, sentience or justified responsibility.
findings.previous_definition: Willingness to endorse the values or ethical commitments one attributes to an advisor.
findings.revised_definition: Willingness to rely on an agent’s moral judgment or endorse its ethical commitments.
findings.definition_revision_reason: The prior definition covered only advisor-value endorsement from review121. This read source uses the same term for willingness to rely on a moral decision maker. Make the row an explicit umbrella covering both source-defined usages without claiming equivalent scales or adding a duplicate name; preserve the original definition in the source121 record and this revision trail.

findings.definition: Transferring decision-making authority to another party who chooses on one's behalf.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: would you prefer making the decision yourself

findings.evidence_scope: Binary self-versus-robot choice is an explicit hypothetical willingness to delegate in a moral dilemma. Agency/affect descriptions alter its proportion in mixed-effects analyses; the paper calls this measure implicit trust.
findings.boundary: This is not an unconscious association test, live consent or executed delegation. Participants may prefer to avoid a difficult moral decision or blame; the source acknowledges that alternative. Distinguish self-report choice, felt trust, legitimate authorization and actual responsibility.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Agency is explicitly manipulated in stories independently of assigned affect and appearance. Agency predicts hypothetical delegation, explicit trust and capability; the responsibility agency main effect is nonsignificant.
findings.boundary: Narratives about capacities are not proof those capacities exist. Mental-state comprehension demands are also bundled with conditions. Capacity attribution, perceived competence, actual moral agency, sentience and rightful responsibility differ.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: ability to feel and experience the world

findings.evidence_scope: Affect manipulation describes subjective felt experience and influences moral-decision trust/capability and perceived responsibility. Source footnote1 explicitly relates this usage to Gray’s experience dimension.
findings.boundary: Source-specific affect/experience language does not establish all emotions, empathy or genuine robot feeling. The eight-item post-experiment composite is one reported factor; it does not prove universal dimensional identity or that affect is an essential normative condition of accountability.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The study crosses appearance with top-down capacity descriptions. Explicit trust is higher for mechanical robots overall, while appearance’s binary-choice and capability main effects are nonsignificant. Actual three-way interactions qualify combined description effects.
findings.boundary: Human likeness is not universally trust-enhancing or trust-reducing. Appearance classes include only four fixed exemplars each. Attribution effects, liking, safety impressions and actual deserved trust differ; the study does not identify a universal mechanism or curve.

findings.definition: A judgment that an agent or organization has the skills, knowledge and capabilities needed to perform a task adequately.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: A 0–100 item assesses perceived moral-decision capability. Agency/affect and their appearance-dependent combination affect ratings. Figure 3’s capability axis/means match this outcome, despite its explicit-trust caption.
findings.boundary: Perceived competence is not measured moral performance. No actual decision from the robot is shown. Capability and trust have correlated but different measures, and swapped plots must not be pooled under one outcome.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity the capacity to understand moral considerations, make ethical judgments and bear responsibility for its choices.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Conditional perceived responsibility after an imagined sacrifice differs from trust in making the right choice. Affect has a reported main effect on this rating; agency/appearance do not. Supplement punishment judgments remain a separate measure.
findings.boundary: A descriptive responsibility rating does not establish moral understanding, subjective awareness, punishment eligibility, machine rights or a human’s legal defense. Do not infer universal absence of human affect from a diagnosis or erase human/operator duties. The experiment supplies no clinical/legal validation.

findings.definition: A drop in comfort or affinity when an artificial agent appears highly, but imperfectly, human-like, rather than a steady increase as human likeness rises.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use existing trust, delegation, capacity-attribution and competence records. Distinguish source-defined measures and preserve construct boundaries instead of adding an instrument label as a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: an explanation for these results might lie

findings.evidence_scope: Uncanny valley and human-distinctiveness threat are proposed explanations of the unexpected appearance pattern; the source recommends android/baseline follow-up to test them.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only hypothesis. Eeriness, identity threat, a human-likeness continuum and a valley-shaped outcome are not measured. A two-category difference or nondetected combined-attribute increase is not a demonstrated valley, literal scale ceiling or unique causal explanation.

source_corrections.finding: Figure3 is captioned explicit trust but its y axis is capability and low-low point matches capability mean22.79. Figure4 is captioned capability but its y axis is trust and low-low point matches explicit-trust mean25.75. Treat the graphical outcomes as transposed relative to captions/text cross-references; preserve the numerical outcome definitions and do not exchange trust/capability data.

Broad mechanical-more-trusted language extends to implicit trust in discussion, but main results report no appearance main effect and Supplement Table1 gives p=.143. The explicit-trust appearance result p=.018is supported. State this outcome distinction rather than universal mechanical superiority.

Text lists high-versus-low affect with30.93and37.67respectively, contradicting its stated higher-affect benefit and conditional means. The direction/order needs clarification; do not use the reversed respectively labels as verified raw-data estimates.

Dimensions of Mind Perception appears twice with DOI10.1007/s11097-010-9186-7. That DOI is Richard Menary’s2010 Dimensions of mind, not Gray/Gray/Wegner’s Science315:619. Correct the pointer to10.1126/science.1134475and count the repeated bibliography entry once. The Menary article exists; this is a wrong citation target, not a fabricated paper.
Responsible Autonomy’s DOI identifies IJCAI2017,pages4698–4704, not the printed AAMAS venue. Metadata correction only; original proceedings paper unread.
Normalize the printed10.1111/2Fj.1467-9280.2008.02122.x to the resolving10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02122.x. Identity verified; underlying study not independently read.

Publisher byline/citation and Crossref name TetsushiTanibe,TakaakiHashimoto,KaoriKarasawa as authors; JoshBongard is listed as editor. Remove editor from the author list and reduce the doubledhttps://doi.org/ prefix to one canonical DOI link. Header inspection is not a full reading of the cited experiment.
glmer is the model-fitting function in the lme4 R package, rather than lme4 being a function of a glmer package. This naming reversal does not itself refute the reported mixed-effects analyses.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: F(1,183)is repeatedly printed. Under the stated complete184-person2×2between-subject design, a conventional full factorial residual denominator is180; some partial-eta values also do not reconcile exactly with the printed df. Supplement tables provide no df and raw data/code are unavailable. Exact fitted model and corrected statistics remain unverifiable.

The humanoid-subset description includes Agency and Affect slopes within participant even though both factors are assigned between participants. The exact grouping/variance parameterization, fitted formula, singularity and convergence diagnostics require the unavailable code/output. This is an unresolved model-specification question, not proof that all repeated-data analyses are invalid.

The paper reports both but no verified public node/registration file was located. Original fields, timing, exclusions, planned contrasts, random-effects fallback and amendment chronology cannot be independently checked.
The bibliography repeats the Kwan/Fiske author pair; Crossref has no author field for the cited DOI. No independent primary byline checked, so no guessed complete-author correction applied.

The experiment provides no evidence about antisocial personality disorder, every diagnosed person’s affect, criminal responsibility or current jurisdictional defenses. Kinscherff2010 exists and its indexed abstract argues a proposition against blanket exclusion, not proof of universally available insanity defense. Do not adopt this source passage as clinical/legal guidance or infer that affect ratings justify robot punishment.

The paper discusses mediation and affect as essential to moral trust, but reports factorial outcome effects, not an identified mediation model or necessity test. Story framing, mental-state elaboration, demand cues and alternative delegation motives are not excluded.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Formal three-way terms are reported for binary trust, explicit trust and capability. Do not dismiss them as an inference solely from significant versus nonsignificant subgroup effects.

Binary analysis includes participant and item random effects; other outcomes are averaged by person/appearance and use repeated-measures analysis. Reported convergence simplifications are disclosed. A df question is not proof every response was treated as a new participant.
2022online,2023issue and2026repository download are distinct legitimate dates. No future publication or false author identity inferred from filename/cover differences.

DOI10.1109/MRA.2012.2192811resolves to a real2012IEEE Uncanny Valley version. Distinguish it from the original1970Energy reference rather than label the classic fabricated or force an invented original-year DOI. Neither full version was read.
The plotted trust/capability means lie far below the100-point scale maximum. Nonsignificant added benefit is not a demonstrated measurement ceiling or proof of exact saturation.

integrity_audit.scope: Same-context audit of the bounded catalogue interpretation; not independent clinical/legal review or a consequential decision.

charter.Facts: VERIFIED supplied19pages, four figures, two public supplement tables and cited metadata/bylines. INFERRED conventional expected df and figure mapping from axes/means. UNVERIFIABLE original registration/amendment timing, exact fitted outputs and current clinical/legal generalizations.

uses_not_supported: Diagnosing affect or moral worth from a personality-disorder label
Determining an individual’s legal defense or criminal responsibility
Punishing robots or excusing human duties because of perceived feelings
Deploying lethal or clinical autonomy on the basis of vignette trust ratings

methodological_limits: One student sample, four robots per appearance class and hypothetical dilemmas; not real robot interaction, moral performance or broad population representation.

Story manipulations are orthogonal assignment factors but comprehension/perspective-taking content differs in low-low condition. Post ratings combine eight items into one exploratory factor; separate agency/affect manipulation validation is limited.

Binary so-called implicit trust is an explicit choice proxy, with possible moral burden/blame avoidance. There is no response-time implicit measure, actual execution or demonstrated informed consent to real harm.

Mixed/repeated analyses and real three-way interactions are preserved. Reported df inconsistencies, convergence-driven slope reductions, multiple nominal tests and unavailable exact code limit quantitative confidence.

Outcome scales, source-defined moral reliance and value endorsement differ. A common label, correlation or broadly similar pattern does not establish psychological identity or validated scale interchangeability.

Explicit appearance effect does not imply a significant implicit/capability appearance effect. Nondetection is not equivalence, agency irrelevance or exact saturation; scale maxima are not approached.
Eeriness, identity threat, causal mediators and actual machine feelings are unmeasured. A factorial description effect does not establish a universal mechanism or necessity of affect.
Clinical/legal/punishment discussion is not a measured result or current jurisdictional standard. No diagnosis, human moral worth or machine sanction eligibility follows from perceived affect.
Registration/amendment/data/code and cited original studies/books remain unread except the exact available two-table supplement. All access limits and metadata-only corrections remain explicit.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Moral trust there is advisor-value endorsement; here it is moral-decision reliance. Revise the row into an explicit umbrella and retain both source-defined operational meanings rather than invent another similarly named mechanism or pool incomparable scales.
A one-factor composite in one selected eight-item set does not settle the universal structure of mind perception; preserve alternative structures and operational scope.
Appearance and attributed capacities may have different effects across danger and moral-trust tasks. Actual uncanny mechanisms and genuine capacity require separate tests.

Perceived affect/responsibility and theoretical blame accounts do not establish justified punishment, legal personhood or clinical claims. The previously corrected final2023Nijssen citation is corroborated here.
Delegation choices, trust ratings, capability and fairness are different outcomes. Keep source choice versus evaluation distinctions and proper repeated-data analyses.

deferred.term: Implicit trust / Explicit trust as two new behaviors
deferred.reason: Source labels denote a binary hypothetical choice and a slider rating, not two independently identified psychological mechanisms. Retain as source-specific measures in existing trust/delegation records.

deferred.term: Affective-state attribution as a new synonym row
deferred.reason: Source footnote explicitly relates this to experience attribution; enrich existing record with scope rather than duplicate it.

deferred.term: Uncanny valley / identity threat / ceiling effect as newly demonstrated mechanisms
deferred.reason: Unmeasured explanations; the added-attribute null is not a literal measurement ceiling.

deferred.term: Insanity defense, affective necessity or punishment eligibility as behavior findings
deferred.reason: Unvalidated normative/clinical/legal extrapolation, not results of this human observer experiment.

limitations: No new entries, categories or ethical principles. Eight existing records enriched, with one explicitly documented definition-scope revision. Stable IDs and unnumbered rows preserved; no source quota, annual-count update, automatic harm edge, independent-audit claim or full-paper Markdown copy.
